specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: CANE proposes context-aware network embeddings as a methodological innovation to address the claimed limitation of existing methods that assign fixed, context-free embeddings to vertices. The paper's logical argument chain proceeds from motivation (intuitive examples of diverse vertex roles) → problem formulation (Definition 2 formalizes context-aware embeddings) → technical solution (mutual attention mechanism on text) → empirical validation (link prediction and vertex classification). The core reasoning is coherent but relies heavily on intuitive motivation rather than empirical evidence of failure modes in existing methods. The paper demonstrates strong empirical results on link prediction (Cora/HepTh) but shows diminishing returns on Zhihu, raising questions about generalization. The logical flow is clear, but several critical junctures lack rigorous justification: (1) why mutual attention is the right mechanism for context-awareness, (2) why simple averaging of context-aware embeddings produces high-quality global embeddings, and (3) whether improvements stem from context-awareness or from the attention mechanism design itself. The paper's claim that context-aware embeddings are 'critical' for network analysis is not fully supported by ablation results, which show modest improvements from attention (~1-2% AUC) and comparable vertex classification performance to baselines.
logical_argument_graph: Premise 1 (Motivation): Real-world vertices exhibit diverse roles when interacting with different neighbors [supported by intuitive example: researcher collaborating on diverse topics]
Premise 2 (Problem): Existing NE methods assign fixed context-free embeddings, failing to capture role diversity [stated but not empirically demonstrated]
Premise 3 (Consequence): Fixed embeddings force neighbor embeddings to be close, reducing discriminativeness [illustrated via Fig. 1 example]
Claim C1 (Problem Validity): Context-free embeddings are inadequate for modeling diverse vertex roles [depends on Premises 1-3; uncertainty: no quantitative failure analysis]
Premise 4 (Solution Concept): Context-aware embeddings—dynamic embeddings conditioned on specific neighbors—can address this [Definition 2 formalizes concept]
Premise 5 (Technical Approach): Mutual attention on text information can generate context-aware embeddings [Eqs. 9-12 define mechanism]
Claim C3 (Technical Feasibility): Mutual attention enables effective context-aware embedding generation [depends on Premise 5; uncertainty: no comparison with alternative attention mechanisms]
Premise 6 (Hybrid Framework): Combining structure-based and text-based embeddings via concatenation captures complementary information [Eq. 1-2 define objectives]
Claim C2 (Superiority): Context-aware embeddings more precisely model semantic relationships [depends on Premises 4-6; uncertainty: conceptual claim, empirical validation deferred]
Premise 7 (Empirical Test): Link prediction AUC on held-out edges measures embedding quality [standard evaluation metric]
Claim C4 (Performance Gains): CANE achieves significant improvements on link prediction [Tables 2-4 provide evidence; uncertainty: Zhihu shows smaller gains, no statistical significance testing]
Premise 8 (Aggregation): Simple averaging of context-aware embeddings produces global embeddings [Section 5.5 defines aggregation]
Claim C5 (Generalization): Context-aware embeddings compose high-quality global embeddings [depends on Premise 8; uncertainty: only tested on Cora, averaging is heuristic]
Premise 9 (Stability): CANE maintains consistent improvements across training ratios [Tables 2-4 show trends]
Claim C6 (Robustness): CANE exhibits stable performance across varying training data ratios [depends on Premise 9; uncertainty: stability metric not formally defined]

Conclusion (Main Claim): Context-aware embeddings are critical for network analysis, especially link prediction [depends on Claims C1-C6; tension: ablation results suggest incremental rather than critical contribution]

strengths.title: Clear problem reformulation with formal definitions

concerns.title: Motivation lacks empirical evidence of failure modes in existing methods
concerns.description: The paper motivates context-aware embeddings through intuitive examples (researcher collaborations) but provides no empirical analysis of how or when existing context-free methods fail. This weakens the justification for the proposed approach.

No comparison of embedding quality before/after introducing context-awareness on the same baseline method
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add empirical analysis showing specific failure cases of context-free embeddings. For example, analyze cases where CENE (which uses text but not context-awareness) makes incorrect link predictions, and show that CANE corrects these errors due to context-awareness rather than other factors.

counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If context-aware embeddings are truly critical for network analysis, the paper should demonstrate this by showing that existing methods fail on specific types of networks or tasks where context-awareness is essential. specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: CANE proposes context-aware network embeddings—dynamic, neighbor-conditioned vertex representations—as an alternative to fixed context-free embeddings in network embedding models. The core methodological contribution is a mutual attention mechanism applied to text-based information that enables embeddings to vary based on interaction context. The paper combines structure-based embeddings (via LINE-style objectives) with text-based embeddings (via CNN + mutual attention) through concatenation. Empirical validation on link prediction across three datasets (Cora, HepTh, Zhihu) shows improvements over baselines (TADW, CENE), with ablations demonstrating the contribution of attention. However, the methodology rests on several critical assumptions about vertex role diversity and text informativeness that lack rigorous empirical validation. The evaluation exhibits methodological concerns: (1) no statistical significance testing despite modest improvements on some datasets; (2) hyperparameter tuning differs across datasets, raising fairness questions; (3) negative sampling parameter k=1 is unusually low and not justified; (4) vertex classification improvements are marginal (~1%), suggesting context-awareness may be less critical for global embedding tasks; (5) Zhihu results show substantially smaller gains (1–2 AUC points) than Cora/HepTh, indicating dataset-dependent effectiveness. The case study is qualitative and limited to 3 vertex pairs. The paper claims context-aware embeddings are 'critical' for network analysis, but ablation results suggest the contribution is incremental. Reproducibility is hampered by incomplete hyperparameter reporting and lack of code availability disclosure.
logical_argument_graph: Premise 1: Vertices in real-world networks exhibit diverse roles when interacting with different neighbors (motivating example: researcher collaborating on diverse topics).
Premise 2: Existing network embedding methods assign fixed context-free embeddings to all vertices, failing to capture role diversity.
Premise 3: Text information associated with vertices reflects these diverse roles and can be leveraged via attention mechanisms.
Conclusion 1: Context-aware embeddings (dynamic, neighbor-conditioned) should improve semantic relationship modeling.
Premise 4: Mutual attention applied to text-based CNN embeddings can effectively generate context-aware representations.
Premise 5: Combining structure-based and text-based embeddings via concatenation preserves information from both modalities.
Conclusion 2: CANE (structure + text-based embeddings with mutual attention) should outperform baselines on link prediction.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: CANE proposes context-aware network embeddings as an incremental but meaningful refinement of existing network embedding paradigms. The core contribution is conceptual (reframing embeddings as context-dependent rather than context-free) combined with a technical instantiation (mutual attention mechanism on text). The paper extends prior work (TADW, CENE, LINE) by introducing dynamic, neighbor-conditioned embeddings derived from text information. Novelty is moderate: the concept of context-awareness is intuitive and well-motivated, but the technical execution (attention-based pooling of CNN features) is relatively straightforward. The empirical validation is solid on link prediction but shows diminishing returns on vertex classification and weaker improvements on the Zhihu dataset. The contribution is best characterized as incremental refinement with localized innovation in the attention mechanism design, rather than a paradigm shift. The paper demonstrates competent execution but lacks theoretical grounding or surprising empirical insights that would elevate it to disruptive novelty.

transparency_notes: This review assesses novelty through an incremental-contribution lens, which emphasizes how the work extends, refines, or reorganizes existing paradigms. Under this lens, CANE is characterized as a meaningful but incremental refinement of existing network embedding methods.

The creativity safeguard flags that context-aware embeddings lack close analogs in the retrieved literature corpus, which could signal innovation. However, the concept is intuitive and the technical execution (attention-based pooling) is straightforward, suggesting the innovation is localized rather than paradigm-shifting.

The paper's empirical validation is solid on link prediction but shows diminishing returns on vertex classification and weaker improvements on Zhihu. This pattern suggests the contribution is task-specific and dataset-dependent rather than broadly transformative.

The absence of statistical significance testing and the use of unusual hyperparameters (k=1) raise methodological concerns that are orthogonal to novelty assessment but affect confidence in empirical claims.
The case study on attention interpretability is qualitative and limited; expanding it would strengthen claims about the mechanism's effectiveness.

This review acknowledges that incremental contributions can be valuable if they are well-executed and address real problems. CANE appears to be competently executed and addresses a reasonable problem (context-dependent embeddings), but the novelty is moderate and the empirical benefits are mixed.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: CANE introduces a conceptually novel reframing of network embedding as a context-dependent rather than context-free task. The core innovation—assigning dynamic, neighbor-conditioned embeddings to vertices via mutual attention over text—diverges from the fixed-embedding paradigm that dominates prior work. While the paper lacks direct precedent for context-aware embeddings in network representation learning, the idea is coherent and addresses a genuine limitation of existing methods. The contribution is primarily conceptual (problem reformulation) and technical (mutual attention mechanism), supported by empirical validation on link prediction. However, the novelty is tempered by: (1) modest improvements on one dataset (Zhihu: 1–2 AUC points), (2) limited vertex classification gains (~1% from attention), (3) absence of statistical significance testing, and (4) reliance on simple averaging for global embeddings. The paper makes a controlled but incremental advance rather than a disruptive breakthrough. The mutual attention mechanism itself is not novel (attention is well-established in NLP), but its application to network embedding via text-based conditioning is relatively unexplored. The core conceptual claim—that vertices exhibit diverse roles requiring context-aware representations—is intuitive but empirically underdeveloped; no quantitative analysis of failure modes in fixed-embedding methods is provided.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: CANE proposes context-aware network embeddings—dynamic, neighbor-conditioned vertex representations—as an alternative to fixed context-free embeddings. The core claim is that vertices exhibit diverse roles when interacting with different neighbors, and mutual attention mechanisms applied to text information can capture these roles more effectively than existing methods. The paper's evidence chain proceeds from intuitive motivation (researcher collaborations) → formal problem definition (Definition 2) → technical solution (mutual attention on CNN features) → empirical validation (link prediction, vertex classification, case study). Cross-checking against the shared extraction stage and prior reviewer assessments reveals a pattern of partially supported claims with significant uncertainty flags. The link prediction improvements on Cora/HepTh are substantial (3-25 AUC points), but Zhihu shows only 0.6-2.6 point gains, raising generalization concerns. Ablation results indicate attention contributes ~1-2% AUC improvement, suggesting context-awareness is a modest rather than critical factor. The paper's central claim that 'context-aware embeddings are critical for network analysis' is overstated relative to the empirical evidence, particularly given comparable vertex classification performance to baselines and the absence of statistical significance testing. The mutual attention mechanism itself is not novel (attention is well-established in NLP), but its application to network embedding via text-based conditioning is relatively unexplored. The case study is qualitative and limited to 3 vertex pairs, providing weak evidence for the interpretability claim.

consensus_findings: CANE introduces context-aware network embeddings as a conceptually novel reframing of network representation learning, distinguishing itself from fixed context-free embeddings via formal definitions (Definition 1 vs. Definition 2). This problem reformulation is coherent and addresses an intuitive limitation of prior work.

The paper provides comprehensive empirical evaluation across three datasets (Cora, HepTh, Zhihu) with varying training ratios (15%-95% edge removal), demonstrating broad empirical coverage and robustness across different data sparsity levels.

Link prediction improvements are substantial on citation networks (Cora: 3-25 AUC points; HepTh: 3-4 AUC points) but substantially smaller on Q&A platform (Zhihu: 0.6-2.6 AUC points), indicating dataset-dependent effectiveness.

Ablation studies (CANE text-only, CANE w/o attention) demonstrate component contributions, with attention contributing approximately 1-2% AUC improvement, suggesting context-awareness is a modest rather than critical factor.
Vertex classification improvements are marginal (~1% from attention), suggesting context-aware embeddings may be less critical for tasks requiring global representations.

The mutual attention mechanism is a straightforward application of established attention techniques (CNN + correlation-based attention + softmax) to network embedding, representing incremental rather than disruptive technical novelty.

The paper lacks statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, and multiple runs with different random seeds, making it unclear whether observed improvements are statistically meaningful, particularly on Zhihu.

Hyperparameter tuning differs across datasets (α, β, γ values vary), and baseline tuning effort is not documented, raising fairness concerns. Negative sampling parameter k=1 is unusually low compared to standard practice (k≥5).

The case study (Section 5.6, Fig. 4) is qualitative and limited to 3 vertex pairs, providing weak evidence for interpretability claims. No analysis of failure cases or quantitative metrics for attention alignment.

The paper's claim that context-aware embeddings are 'critical' for network analysis is overstated relative to empirical evidence, particularly given modest Zhihu improvements, marginal vertex classification gains, and the absence of significance testing.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: CANE proposes context-aware network embeddings—dynamic, neighbor-conditioned vertex representations—as an alternative to fixed context-free embeddings in network representation learning. The paper introduces a coherent problem reformulation (Definitions 1–2) distinguishing context-free from context-aware embeddings, proposes a mutual attention mechanism applied to text-based information to generate context-aware representations, and provides comprehensive empirical evaluation across three datasets (Cora, HepTh, Zhihu) with varying training ratios. The conceptual contribution is genuine and addresses an intuitive limitation of prior work. However, empirical evidence is mixed: link prediction improvements are substantial on citation networks (Cora: 3–25 AUC points; HepTh: 3–4 points) but substantially smaller on Q&A platform (Zhihu: 0.6–2.6 points). Ablation studies show attention contributes only 1–2% AUC improvement, and vertex classification gains are marginal (~1%), suggesting context-awareness is incremental rather than critical. The paper lacks statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, and multiple runs, making it unclear whether improvements are statistically meaningful. Hyperparameter tuning fairness is questionable (different α, β, γ across datasets; k=1 negative sampling unusually low). The mutual attention mechanism is a straightforward application of established techniques rather than a novel technical contribution. The case study is qualitative and limited to 3 vertex pairs. Overall, the paper makes a controlled but incremental methodological advance with moderate conceptual novelty, comprehensive but methodologically limited empirical evaluation, and overstated claims about the 'criticality' of context-aware embeddings.
strengths: Clear problem reformulation with formal definitions: Definitions 1–2 provide precise, unambiguous distinction between context-free and context-aware embeddings, enabling clear communication of the core contribution and facilitating reproducibility.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple datasets and training ratios: Evaluation on three datasets (Cora, HepTh, Zhihu) with 9 training ratios (15%–95% edge removal) demonstrates broad empirical coverage and robustness across different data sparsity levels.
Well-designed ablation studies: Three variants (CANE text-only, CANE w/o attention, CANE) isolate contributions of different components, enabling assessment of individual factor importance.

Interpretability via attention weight visualization: Case study (Section 5.6, Fig. 4) provides qualitative evidence that attention weights align with semantically meaningful words, offering interpretability into model decision-making.
Principled integration of structure and text: Separate objectives (Ls, Lt) with explicit weighting parameters (α, β, γ) enable flexible control over contribution of different information sources.

Consistent improvements on link prediction across datasets: CANE outperforms baselines on link prediction across all three datasets and most training ratios, suggesting broad applicability for this task.
limitations: Zhihu dataset shows substantially smaller improvements (0.6–2.6 AUC points) compared to Cora/HepTh (3–25 points), raising critical generalization concerns. The paper provides no analysis of dataset properties (network density, text quality, vertex degree distribution) that might explain this dramatic difference, leaving unclear whether context-aware embeddings are necessary for all network types or only for citation networks with high-quality text.

Ablation study reveals attention mechanism contributes only 1–2% AUC improvement, suggesting context-awareness is a modest refinement rather than a critical innovation. This directly contradicts the paper's claim that context-aware embeddings are 'critical for network analysis.' The majority of improvements may derive from combining structure and text via concatenation, not from context-aware conditioning.

Absence of statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple runs with different random seeds undermines confidence in reported improvements. Zhihu improvements (0.6–2.6 AUC points) are particularly vulnerable to noise and could be within typical variance margins for embedding methods. Without significance testing, it is impossible to determine whether observed improvements are statistically meaningful.

Hyperparameter tuning fairness is unclear: different α, β, γ values across datasets without documented justification; baseline tuning effort not specified; negative sampling parameter k=1 is unusually low compared to standard practice (k≥5), potentially biasing results in favor of CANE. These methodological choices raise questions about whether comparisons are fair.

Vertex classification improvements are marginal (~1% from attention), suggesting context-aware embeddings may be less critical for tasks requiring global representations. Simple averaging of context-aware embeddings achieves comparable performance to baselines, not superior performance, undermining the claim that context-aware embeddings 'compose' high-quality global embeddings.

(4) Hyperparameter fairness is unclear (different α, β, γ across datasets; k=1 negative sampling unusually low). (7) Mutual attention is straightforward application of established techniques, not novel technical contribution. The paper makes a controlled but incremental advance suitable for specialized venues focused on network embedding methods. For acceptance at top-tier venues, the paper would need: (a) statistical significance testing with confidence intervals, (b) fair hyperparameter tuning for all baselines, (c) analysis of dataset properties affecting CANE's effectiveness, (d) comparison with alternative attention mechanisms, (e) expanded case study with quantitative metrics, (f) revised claims reflecting incremental rather than critical contribution. human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
CANE proposes context-aware network embeddings—dynamic, neighbor-conditioned vertex representations generated via mutual attention over text information—as an alternative to fixed context-free embeddings. The paper provides clear formal definitions (Definition 1 vs. Definition 2), proposes a mutual attention mechanism applied to CNN-based text embeddings, and evaluates the approach on three datasets (Cora, HepTh, Zhihu) with varying training ratios. The conceptual contribution is coherent and addresses an intuitive limitation of prior work. However, empirical evidence is mixed: substantial improvements on citation networks (Cora: 3–25 AUC points; HepTh: 3–4 points) but substantially smaller on Q&A platform (Zhihu: 0.6–2.6 points). Ablation studies show attention contributes only 1–2% AUC improvement, and vertex classification gains are marginal (~1%), suggesting context-awareness is incremental rather than critical. The paper lacks statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, and multiple runs, making it unclear whether improvements are statistically meaningful. Hyperparameter tuning fairness is questionable (different α, β, γ across datasets; k=1 negative sampling unusually low). The mutual attention mechanism is a straightforward application of established techniques. The case study is qualitative and limited to 3 vertex pairs. Overall, the paper makes a controlled but incremental methodological advance with moderate conceptual novelty and comprehensive but methodologically limited empirical evaluation.

Strengths:
1. Clear problem reformulation with formal definitions: Definitions 1–2 provide precise distinction between context-free and context-aware embeddings, enabling clear communication and facilitating reproducibility.
2. Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Three datasets with 9 training ratios (15%–95% edge removal) demonstrate broad empirical coverage and robustness across different data sparsity levels.
3. Well-designed ablation studies: Three variants (CANE text-only, CANE w/o attention, CANE) isolate contributions of different components, enabling assessment of individual factor importance.
4. Interpretability via attention visualization: Case study (Section 5.6, Fig. 4) provides qualitative evidence that attention weights align with semantically meaningful words, offering interpretability into model decision-making.
5. Principled integration of structure and text: Separate objectives (Ls, Lt) with explicit weighting parameters (α, β, γ) enable flexible control over contribution of different information sources.
6. Consistent improvements on link prediction: CANE outperforms baselines on link prediction across all three datasets and most training ratios, suggesting broad applicability for this task.

Limitations:
1. Zhihu dataset shows substantially smaller improvements (0.6–2.6 AUC points) compared to Cora/HepTh (3–25 points), raising critical generalization concerns. The paper provides no analysis of dataset properties (network density, text quality, vertex degree distribution) that might explain this dramatic difference, leaving unclear whether context-aware embeddings are necessary for all network types or only for citation networks with high-quality text. This is a major concern for the generalizability of the proposed approach.
2. Ablation study reveals attention mechanism contributes only 1–2% AUC improvement, suggesting context-awareness is a modest refinement rather than a critical innovation. This directly contradicts the paper's claim that context-aware embeddings are 'critical for network analysis.' The majority of improvements may derive from combining structure and text via concatenation, not from context-aware conditioning. This undermines the core motivation for the work.
3. Absence of statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple runs with different random seeds undermines confidence in reported improvements. Zhihu improvements (0.6–2.6 AUC points) are particularly vulnerable to noise and could be within typical variance margins for embedding methods. Without significance testing, it is impossible to determine whether observed improvements are statistically meaningful. This is a critical methodological gap.

Open Questions:
1. Why does Zhihu dataset show 0.6–2.6 AUC point improvements while Cora/HepTh show 3–25 points? What dataset properties (network density, text quality, vertex degree distribution, edge weight distribution) correlate with CANE's effectiveness? Is context-aware embedding beneficial primarily for citation networks with high-quality text, or does it generalize to other network types? This question is essential for understanding the scope and applicability of the proposed approach.
2. If attention mechanism contributes only 1–2% AUC improvement, what is the primary driver of the 3–25 AUC point improvements on Cora/HepTh? Is it the combination of structure and text via concatenation, or is it the specific attention-based text encoding? Would a simpler baseline combining structure and text without attention achieve similar results? This question is critical for understanding whether context-awareness is the key innovation or whether simpler alternatives could achieve similar results.
3. Are the reported improvements statistically significant? What are the 95% confidence intervals for AUC values? How do results vary across multiple runs with different random seeds? Without significance testing, it is unclear whether improvements are meaningful or within noise. This is essential for validating the empirical claims.
4. How do alternative attention mechanisms (additive vs. multiplicative, single vs. mutual, different pooling strategies) compare to the proposed mutual attention? Is the proposed design optimal, or could simpler alternatives achieve similar results? Why were specific design choices (mean-pooling, tanh activation) made? This question is important for understanding whether the technical contribution is well-justified.
5. Why is vertex classification only evaluated on Cora? Do context-aware embeddings improve vertex classification on HepTh and Zhihu? If not, does this indicate that context-awareness is task-specific (beneficial for link prediction but not for global embedding tasks)? What explains the marginal improvement from attention (~1%)? This question is important for understanding the scope of applicability.

Transparency:
The paper exhibits significant transparency gaps that limit confidence in the reported results. Statistical rigor is lacking: no confidence intervals, p-values, or significance tests are reported; no documentation of multiple runs or cross-validation procedure is provided. Hyperparameter tuning details are incomplete: grid search procedure is mentioned but not fully documented; search space, validation procedure, and baseline tuning effort are not specified; different hyperparameter values across datasets (α, β, γ) are used without explanation. The negative sampling parameter k=1 is unusually low compared to standard practice (k≥5), and the justification ('to speed up training') suggests potential bias toward CANE. Dataset properties are not analyzed: no investigation of network density, text quality, vertex degree distribution, or other properties that might explain why Zhihu shows smaller improvements. Attention mechanism design choices are not justified: mean-pooling vs. max-pooling is mentioned but not ablated; tanh activation is used without justification or comparison with alternatives; no comparison with other attention mechanisms is provided. The case study is limited in scope: only 3 vertex pairs from Cora are shown; no examples from HepTh or Zhihu; no quantitative metrics for evaluating attention alignment; no analysis of failure cases. Vertex classification evaluation is incomplete: only evaluated on Cora; no results on HepTh or Zhihu; no justification for why evaluation is limited to one dataset. Reproducibility is hampered: no disclosure of code availability; implementation details are incomplete (CNN architecture, word embedding initialization, training hyperparameters beyond α, β, γ are not specified). Baseline tuning is not documented: no documentation of hyperparameter tuning effort for baselines (TADW, CENE, DeepWalk, LINE, node2vec); unclear whether baselines received equivalent tuning effort as CANE. Motivation empirical grounding is weak: intuitive examples are provided but no quantitative analysis of failure modes in existing methods; no empirical evidence that fixed embeddings actually fail to capture diverse roles in practice.

While 2-way models were shown to have very good performances on some KB datasets, they have limited expressiveness and they can fail dramatically on harder datasets. In contrast, 3-way models perform some form of low-rank tensor factorization, and in that respect can have extremely high expressiveness depending on the rank constraints. In the 718 Embedding Models for Link Prediction in KBs context of link prediction for multi-relational data, RESCAL (Nickel, Tresp, & Kriegel, 2011) follows natural modeling assumptions. Similarly to TransE, RESCAL learns one low-dimensional embedding for each entity. However, relationships are represented as a bilinear operator in the embedding space in RESCAL, i.e. each relationship corresponds to a matrix, whereas in TransE they are also represented by vectors. Besides the diﬀerent interactions across the arguments of a triple to explain its validity, these models also diﬀer in their training objective. The training objective of RESCAL is the Frobenius norm between the original data tensor and its low-rank reconstruction, whereas Tatec uses the margin ranking criterion of TransE. Another related 3-way model is SME(bilinear) (Bordes et al., 2013a). The parameterization of SME(bilinear) is a constrained version of RESCAL, and also uses a ranking criterion as training objective.

There is already a policy on review incentives and sanctions, including temporary bans on (re-)submission or commitment to ACL venues. To add to the above points, the reviews that look like they were written by ChatGPT overall decrease the faith in the peer review process. According to this study, there is more generated text in ‘reviews which report lower confidence, were submitted close to the deadline, and from reviewers who are less likely to respond to author rebuttals’. All these factors generally correspond to the type of unmotivated reviewer that, as authors, we would prefer to avoid. The increased ratio of such reviews also attunes the community to reviews that sound like they were generated. Generally, reviews are valued for their content rather than language, so your thoughts are more likely to be appreciated if they come in your voice (even if with linguistic imperfections). Finally: some authors actually count on you to use generative AI, and include hidden prompt injections intended to manipulate your assistant into giving a positive review! If you notice anything like that, please raise it with the chairs, such submissions should be desk rejected. What about the authors, can they use generative AI? The ACL policy on publication ethics discusses various cases with different degrees of acceptability.

Section: Q: Can I use generative AI?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, policy_screen
Content: cs committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct. There is already a policy on review incentives and sanctions, including temporary bans on (re-)submission or commitment to ACL venues. To add to the above points, the reviews that look like they were written by ChatGPT overall decrease the faith in the peer review process. According to this study, there is more generated text in ‘reviews which report lower confidence, were submitted close to the deadline, and from reviewers who are less likely to respond to author rebuttals’. All these factors generally correspond to the type of unmotivated reviewer that, as authors, we would prefer to avoid. The increased ratio of such reviews also attunes the community to reviews that sound like they were generated. Generally, reviews are valued for their content rather than language, so your thoughts are more likely to be appreciated if they come in your voice (even if with linguistic imperfections). Finally: some authors actually count on you to use generative AI, and include hidden prompt injections intended to manipulate your assistant into giving a positive review! If you notice anything like that, please raise it with the chairs, such submissions should be desk rejected. What about the authors, can they use generative AI? The ACL policy on publication ethics discusses various cases with different degrees of acceptability.

Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

Hallucinated references or citations: Please check carefully for hallucinated references, which pose a serious concern to scientific reliability. Anonymity violations. As of January 2024, non-anonymous pre-prints are permitted for ARR, but submissions should still be properly anonymized (e.g., not containing explicit references to the authors’ prior work, acknowledgements, links to non-anonymous repositories or services like Dropbox that may track who opened the link). Style guides or length violations: the paper should be desk-rejected if it does not follow the style guides or goes over the page limit (4 pages for short, 8 for long papers, excluding the ethical considerations and limitations).
